# Chapter 3: Naming Guidelines — 3.1–3.2

Rules that no analyzer enforces (judgment), CONSIDER rules that analyzers only suggest, and rules that analyzers check only in part, marked "(partly checked)". Open the examples file for the explanation and code the book gives with each rule.

## 3.1.1 Capitalization Rules for Identifiers

- **FDG3001** DO use PascalCasing for the names of namespaces, types, members, and generic type parameters. (partly checked) (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch03-naming-3-1-to-3-2.md#fdg3001
- **FDG3002** DO use camelCasing for parameter names. (partly checked) (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch03-naming-3-1-to-3-2.md#fdg3002

## 3.1.2 Capitalizing Acronyms

- **FDG3003** DO capitalize both characters of two-character acronyms, except the first word of a camel-cased identifier. (partly checked) (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch03-naming-3-1-to-3-2.md#fdg3003
- **FDG3004** DO capitalize only the first character of acronyms with three or more characters, except the first word of a camel-cased identifier. (partly checked) (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch03-naming-3-1-to-3-2.md#fdg3004
- **FDG3005** DO NOT capitalize any of the characters of any acronyms, whatever their length, at the beginning of a camel-cased identifier. (partly checked) (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch03-naming-3-1-to-3-2.md#fdg3005

## 3.1.3 Capitalizing Compound Words and Common Terms

- **FDG3006** DO NOT capitalize each word in so-called closed-form compound words. (partly checked) (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch03-naming-3-1-to-3-2.md#fdg3006

## 3.2.1 Word Choice

- **FDG3008** DO choose easily readable identifier names. (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch03-naming-3-1-to-3-2.md#fdg3008
- **FDG3009** DO favor readability over brevity. The property name `CanScrollHorizontally` is better than `ScrollableX` (an obscure reference to the *X*-axis). (not in test projects)
- **FDG3010** DO NOT use underscores, hyphens, or any other non-alphanumeric characters. (partly checked) (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch03-naming-3-1-to-3-2.md#fdg3010
- **FDG3011** DO NOT use Hungarian notation. (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch03-naming-3-1-to-3-2.md#fdg3011
- **FDG3012** AVOID using identifiers that conflict with keywords of widely used programming languages. (partly checked) (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch03-naming-3-1-to-3-2.md#fdg3012
- **FDG3013** DO use only ASCII characters in identifier names. (partly checked) (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch03-naming-3-1-to-3-2.md#fdg3013

## 3.2.2 Using Abbreviations and Acronyms

- **FDG3014** DO NOT use abbreviations or contractions as part of identifier names. (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch03-naming-3-1-to-3-2.md#fdg3014
- **FDG3015** DO NOT use any acronyms that are not widely accepted, and even if they are, only when necessary. (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch03-naming-3-1-to-3-2.md#fdg3015

## 3.2.3 Avoiding Language-Specific Names

- **FDG3016** DO use semantically interesting names rather than language-specific keywords for type names. (partly checked) (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch03-naming-3-1-to-3-2.md#fdg3016
- **FDG3017** DO use a generic CLR type name, rather than a language-specific name, in the rare cases when an identifier has no semantic meaning beyond its type. (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch03-naming-3-1-to-3-2.md#fdg3017
- **FDG3018** DO use a common name, such as *value* or *item*, rather than repeating the type name, in the rare cases when an identifier has no semantic meaning and the type of the parameter is not important. (partly checked) (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch03-naming-3-1-to-3-2.md#fdg3018

## 3.2.4 Naming New Versions of Existing APIs

- **FDG3019** DO use a name similar to the old API when creating new versions of an existing API. (library only) — examples: examples/ch03-naming-3-1-to-3-2.md#fdg3019
- **FDG3020** DO prefer adding a suffix rather than a prefix to indicate a new version of an existing API. (library only) — examples: examples/ch03-naming-3-1-to-3-2.md#fdg3020
- **FDG3021** CONSIDER using a brand-new, but meaningful, identifier, instead of adding a suffix or a prefix. (library only)
- **FDG3022** DO use a numeric suffix to indicate a new version of an existing API, particularly if the existing name of the API is the only name that makes sense (e.g., if it is an industry standard) and if adding any meaningful suffix (or changing the name) is not an appropriate option. (library only) — examples: examples/ch03-naming-3-1-to-3-2.md#fdg3022
- **FDG3023** DO NOT use the “Ex” (or a similar) suffix for an identifier to distinguish it from an earlier version of the same API. (partly checked) (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch03-naming-3-1-to-3-2.md#fdg3023
- **FDG3024** DO use the “64” suffix when introducing versions of APIs that operate on a 64-bit integer (a long integer) instead of a 32-bit integer. You only need to take this approach when the existing 32-bit API exists; don’t do it for brand-new APIs with only a 64-bit version. (library only) — examples: examples/ch03-naming-3-1-to-3-2.md#fdg3024
